newsitem.title: TURKEY: Bankers positive on Turkey economy over sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Bankers positive on Turkey economy over sell-offs.

text.p: Turkish bankers and analysts are optimistic for the ailing economy following the approval of a key telecommunications sell-off but warn the government not to rest on its laurels if it wants permanent improvement.
"Now the crown jewel of Turkey's privatisation programme can be sold," Atilla Yesilada, director of research at Global Securities, told Reuters.

"The government has acted very rationally and kick-started the privatisation programme...Without privatisation the fiscal imbalances would have pushed Turkey into a financial crisis very similar to the one that we had in 1994," Yesilada said.
But some analysts warn that the government is only working for a short-term fix, and could be ignoring the need for structural overhaul.
Izzettin Onder, economics professor at Istanbul University, said the government was storing up problems for later by just relying on sell-offs and selling profitable enterprises first.
Bankers say the government has been given a few months' breathing space to put things right amid the euphoria.

It must now work towards sweeping tax reform, reducing tax rates but widening the tax base and improving collection, reform the state-run retirement and health funds and increase social security contributions, and reduce agricultural subsidies.

What it must not do, they say, is bow to pressure and give public workers the high pay rises they are currently demanding. In current bargaining the government is offering state workers a 65 percent rise against a demand of 135 percent.
Turkey's constitutional court last week ruled in favour of privatising Turk Telekom, a sale it had blocked in the past.

Analysts say the first tranche of up to 10 percent could bring in $3.5 billion in the second half of 1997. The government also aims to privatise big petroleum and steel companies and expects an additional $5 billion from sell-offs this year.
Turkey suffered a major financial crisis in 1994 following the downgrading of its credit rating by two major agencies -- Standard and Poor's and Moody's.
Last month, three agencies downgraded Turkey's foreign debt because of worsening fiscal balances. Moody's said it may follow.
But bankers say this time the Telekom decision and related market optimism will cancel out any bad feeling in the market.

"The downgrading...was important but privatisation is even more important, because foreign investors regarded privatisation as the main obstacle for (reducing) the budget deficit," said Oner Ayan, at the international division of Ata Securities.

"After Turk Telekom, after the main obstacle was abolished, then Eregli Demir Celik and Tupras and other locomotives in Turkey will go on to be privatised, and this means that foreign investors can believe in Turkey's future," Ayan said.
The Telekom decision boosted optimism in the markets over what bankers see as the Islamist-led government's determination over privatisation.
"The government's decisiveness on this issue has surprised everyone," Yesilada said. "Since 1986 every administration has promised rapid privatisation, but nobody has delivered so far."
Privatisation has raised only $3 billion since 1986, when the then prime minister Turgut Ozal launched the sell-off plan.

"I don't know if (the government) will reach the target of a balanced budget in 1997 -- but I think if substantial cuts can be made in the budget deficit in real terms, we will see many of the economic indicators improving," Yesilada said.
Finance Minister Abdullatif Sener last week said the 1996 budget deficit was 1,215 trillion lira ($10.6 billion), improved from an earlier estimate of 1,300 trillion lira.
Bond yields have dropped more than 20 points in the past month to around 85 percent, against inflation of 80 percent.
